name: Haemoglobin
what: Haemoglobin is the protein inside red blood cells that carries oxygen from your lungs to the rest of your body.
low_means: A low level is called anaemia. It can come from low iron, low vitamin B12 or folate, blood loss, or long-term illness, and can make you feel tired or breathless.
high_means: A high level can happen with dehydration, smoking, living at high altitude, or conditions that make the body produce extra red cells.

name: Red blood cell count
what: This counts how many red blood cells are in a small amount of blood. Red cells carry oxygen.
low_means: A low count often goes together with anaemia.
high_means: A high count can be caused by dehydration, smoking or conditions that raise red cell production.

name: White blood cell count
what: White blood cells are part of the immune system and help the body fight infections.
low_means: A low count can follow some viral infections, certain medicines, or problems with the bone marrow, and can make infections more likely.
high_means: A high count is most often a sign the body is fighting an infection or inflammation; stress and some medicines can also raise it.

name: Platelet count
what: Platelets are tiny cells that help blood clot and stop bleeding.
low_means: A low count can cause easy bruising or bleeding. In India it is commonly seen with dengue and other viral fevers.
high_means: A high count can happen after infection, inflammation, iron deficiency or, less often, a bone-marrow condition.

name: Haematocrit (PCV)
what: Haematocrit is the share of your blood volume made up of red blood cells.
low_means: A low value usually goes with anaemia.
high_means: A high value is often due to dehydration.

name: MCV
what: MCV is the average size of your red blood cells.
low_means: Small red cells are often linked with iron deficiency.
high_means: Large red cells can be linked with low vitamin B12 or folate, alcohol use, or liver problems.

name: MCH
what: MCH is the average amount of haemoglobin inside each red blood cell.
low_means: A low value is often seen with iron deficiency.
high_means: A high value can go with large red cells, for example from low B12 or folate.

name: MCHC
what: MCHC shows how concentrated the haemoglobin is inside red cells.
low_means: A low value is often linked with iron deficiency.
high_means: A high value is uncommon and can be a lab artefact or a rare red-cell condition.

name: Neutrophils
what: Neutrophils are the most common white cells and are the first to respond to bacterial infections.
low_means: A low share can follow viral infections or some medicines.
high_means: A high share often points to a bacterial infection or inflammation.

name: Lymphocytes
what: Lymphocytes are white cells that help fight viruses and make antibodies.
low_means: A low share can be seen with stress, steroids or some infections.
high_means: A high share is common during viral infections.

name: ESR
what: ESR measures how quickly red cells settle in a tube. It is a general, non-specific sign of inflammation.
low_means: A low ESR is usually not a concern.
high_means: A high ESR suggests inflammation or infection somewhere in the body but does not say where; age and anaemia can also raise it.

name: C-reactive protein
what: CRP is a protein the liver makes when there is inflammation in the body.
low_means: A low CRP is normal.
high_means: A raised CRP points to inflammation or infection. It does not tell the cause.

name: Fasting blood glucose
what: This measures the sugar (glucose) in your blood after not eating for at least 8 hours.
low_means: Low sugar can cause shakiness, sweating or confusion and needs attention, especially in people on diabetes medicine.
high_means: Values from 100 to 125 mg/dL are often called prediabetes; 126 mg/dL or more on repeat tests can indicate diabetes. A doctor confirms this with repeat or other tests.

name: Post-meal blood glucose
what: This measures blood sugar about two hours after a meal.
low_means: Low sugar after eating is uncommon and worth discussing with a doctor.
high_means: A high value after meals can be an early sign the body is not handling sugar well.

name: Random blood glucose
what: This measures blood sugar at any time of day, regardless of meals.
low_means: Low sugar can cause shakiness or confusion.
high_means: A random value of 200 mg/dL or more with symptoms can suggest diabetes and needs follow-up.

name: HbA1c
what: HbA1c reflects your average blood sugar over roughly the last 2–3 months.
low_means: A low value is uncommon and usually not a concern on its own.
high_means: 5.7–6.4% is usually called prediabetes and 6.5% or more can indicate diabetes. It is also used to track how well diabetes is controlled.

name: Total cholesterol
what: This is the total amount of cholesterol, a fatty substance, in your blood.
low_means: Low total cholesterol is usually not a concern.
high_means: High cholesterol can build up in blood vessels over time and raise the risk of heart disease and stroke.

name: LDL cholesterol
what: LDL is often called 'bad' cholesterol because extra LDL can stick to the walls of blood vessels.
low_means: Low LDL is generally considered good.
high_means: High LDL raises the long-term risk of heart attack and stroke. Diet, exercise and sometimes medicine can lower it.

name: HDL cholesterol
what: HDL is often called 'good' cholesterol because it helps carry extra cholesterol away from blood vessels.
low_means: Low HDL is linked with a higher risk of heart disease. Exercise and stopping smoking can raise it.
high_means: Higher HDL is usually considered protective.

name: Triglycerides
what: Triglycerides are a type of fat in the blood that stores extra energy from food.
low_means: Low triglycerides are usually not a concern.
high_means: High levels are linked with heart disease risk; very high levels can inflame the pancreas. Sugar, refined carbs and alcohol raise them.

name: VLDL cholesterol
what: VLDL is a particle that carries triglycerides in the blood.
low_means: Low VLDL is usually not a concern.
high_means: High VLDL usually goes with high triglycerides.

name: Serum creatinine
what: Creatinine is a waste product from muscles that healthy kidneys filter out of the blood.
low_means: Low creatinine can be seen in people with low muscle mass and is usually not a concern.
high_means: A high level can mean the kidneys are not filtering as well as they should. Dehydration and some medicines can also raise it.

name: Blood urea
what: Urea is a waste product formed when the body breaks down protein; the kidneys remove it.
low_means: Low urea can occur with low protein intake or liver problems.
high_means: High urea can come from dehydration, a high-protein diet or reduced kidney function.

name: Blood urea nitrogen
what: BUN measures the nitrogen part of urea in the blood, another marker of kidney function.
low_means: Low BUN is usually not a concern.
high_means: High BUN can come from dehydration or reduced kidney function.

name: eGFR
what: eGFR estimates how well your kidneys filter blood each minute.
low_means: A value below 60 for three months or more can indicate chronic kidney disease; below 15 is kidney failure range.
high_means: A high eGFR is usually not a concern.

name: Uric acid
what: Uric acid is a waste product from breaking down purines, found in some foods and in body cells.
low_means: Low uric acid is uncommon and usually not a concern.
high_means: High uric acid can cause gout (painful joints) or kidney stones.

name: Sodium
what: Sodium is a salt that helps control water balance, nerves and muscles.
low_means: Low sodium can cause headache, confusion or tiredness and has many causes, including some medicines and drinking a lot of water.
high_means: High sodium usually means the body is short of water (dehydration).

name: Potassium
what: Potassium is a mineral that keeps the heart and muscles working properly.
low_means: Low potassium can cause weakness, cramps or an irregular heartbeat; vomiting, diarrhoea and some water pills can cause it.
high_means: High potassium can affect heart rhythm and can be linked with kidney problems or some medicines.

name: Chloride
what: Chloride works with sodium to keep body fluids balanced.
low_means: Low chloride can happen with vomiting or some medicines.
high_means: High chloride can happen with dehydration.

name: Calcium
what: Calcium keeps bones and teeth strong and helps nerves, muscles and the heart work.
low_means: Low calcium can come from low vitamin D or low protein (albumin) and may cause tingling or cramps.
high_means: High calcium can come from overactive parathyroid glands or other conditions and should be checked.

name: TSH
what: TSH is a hormone from the brain's pituitary gland that tells the thyroid how much hormone to make.
low_means: A low TSH often means the thyroid is overactive (hyperthyroidism).
high_means: A high TSH often means the thyroid is underactive (hypothyroidism), which can cause tiredness, weight gain and feeling cold.

name: Total T3
what: T3 is one of the active thyroid hormones that controls how fast the body uses energy.
low_means: Low T3 can go with an underactive thyroid or serious illness.
high_means: High T3 can go with an overactive thyroid.

name: Total T4
what: T4 is the main hormone made by the thyroid gland.
low_means: Low T4 can mean an underactive thyroid.
high_means: High T4 can mean an overactive thyroid.

name: ALT (SGPT)
what: ALT is an enzyme found mainly in the liver.
low_means: A low ALT is normal.
high_means: A raised ALT can mean the liver is irritated or injured, for example from fatty liver, alcohol, hepatitis or some medicines.

name: AST (SGOT)
what: AST is an enzyme found in the liver, heart and muscles.
low_means: A low AST is normal.
high_means: A raised AST can come from liver injury, heavy exercise or muscle damage.

name: Alkaline phosphatase
what: ALP is an enzyme found in the liver and bones.
low_means: Low ALP is uncommon and usually not a concern.
high_means: High ALP can come from blocked bile flow, liver disease or bone growth and bone conditions.

name: Total bilirubin
what: Bilirubin is a yellow substance made when old red blood cells break down; the liver clears it.
low_means: Low bilirubin is usually not a concern.
high_means: High bilirubin can cause yellow skin or eyes (jaundice) and can come from liver problems, blocked bile ducts or fast red-cell breakdown.

name: Albumin
what: Albumin is the main protein made by the liver; it keeps fluid inside blood vessels.
low_means: Low albumin can come from liver or kidney disease, poor nutrition or long illness and can cause swelling.
high_means: High albumin usually means dehydration.

name: Total protein
what: Total protein measures albumin and globulin proteins together.
low_means: Low protein can come from poor nutrition, liver or kidney disease.
high_means: High protein can come from dehydration or long-term inflammation.

name: Vitamin D (25-OH)
what: Vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium and keeps bones and muscles healthy.
low_means: Low vitamin D is very common, especially with little sun exposure, and can cause bone pain or weakness over time. 20–29 ng/mL is often called insufficient and below 20 deficient.
high_means: Very high levels usually come from taking too many supplements.

name: Vitamin B12
what: Vitamin B12 is needed to make red blood cells and keep nerves healthy.
low_means: Low B12 is common in vegetarians and older adults and can cause anaemia, tiredness, tingling or memory problems.
high_means: High B12 is usually from supplements and rarely a concern on its own.

name: Serum iron
what: This measures the iron in your blood. Iron is needed to make haemoglobin.
low_means: Low iron is a common cause of anaemia.
high_means: High iron can come from supplements or conditions where the body stores too much iron.

name: Ferritin
what: Ferritin is the protein that stores iron; it shows how much iron the body has in reserve.
low_means: Low ferritin is the most specific sign of low iron stores.
high_means: High ferritin can come from inflammation, liver disease or iron overload.
